summary: Maps the Policy Core Information Model to a form implementable in a directory accessed through LDAP. It defines structural classes for policy data and relationship classes showing how they connect, plus some classes added only to speed up retrieval of large amounts of policy data. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3703 turns the Policy Core Information Model into an LDAP schema. It defines the directory classes that hold policy rules, groups, conditions and actions, and the ways a rule can point at the conditions and actions it uses.

questions: how to store network policy in ldap
what is the policy core ldap schema
what is a simple policy rule
subtitle: An LDAP schema for storing network policy, so a directory can hold the rules a policy server enforces.

tldr.problem: The Policy Core Information Model describes policy in an object-oriented way, but it says nothing about how those objects are stored. A directory that holds policy needs a schema, and the one defined for X.500 did not fit LDAP.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC maps each structural class of the information model to an LDAP class and each relationship to an attribute, a directory tree placement or an auxiliary class, and adds a set of auxiliary classes that make large retrievals from a directory faster.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3703 is a Proposed Standard from February 2004 and has been updated by RFC 4104.

today: RFC 3703 is a Proposed Standard from February 2004 and has been updated by RFC 4104. It defines the LDAP schema for storing policy data based on the Policy Core Information Model.

sections.title: What the Schema Does
sections.content:
Policy is defined here as a set of rules to administer, manage and control access to network resources. The term is used in that sense throughout, not in the sense used by the directory standards.

The RFC defines a mapping of the Policy Core Information Model to a form that can be implemented in a directory that uses LDAP as its access protocol. The model defines two hierarchies of object classes: structural classes that represent policy information and the control of policies, and relationship classes that show how instances of the structural classes relate to each other. The schema also adds classes that improve the performance of a client retrieving large amounts of policy information from an LDAP server. Those classes exist only to make retrievals faster, and there are no classes in the information model that correspond to them.

For the structural classes, the mapping is one for one: information model classes become LDAP classes, and information model properties become LDAP attributes. For the relationship classes, three mappings are used: LDAP auxiliary classes, attributes that hold distinguished name references, and superior and subordinate relationships in the Directory Information Tree.

Implementations that use an LDAP directory as their policy repository and want to implement policy information according to RFC 3060 must use the schema defined in this document, or a schema that subclasses from it. The schema uses the prefix pcim and contains 23 classes in all.
sections.plainLanguage: The information model describes policy as objects and the relationships between them. This RFC says how to store those objects in an LDAP directory: classes become classes, properties become attributes, and relationships become references or tree positions.

sections.title: The Policy Core Information Model
sections.content:
The RFC contains an LDAP schema representing the classes defined in the companion document, the Policy Core Information Model version 1 specification. Other documents may map the same information model to other storage technologies. Because the detailed semantics of the model classes appear only in that document, the RFC states that it is a prerequisite for reading and understanding this one.

The document itself was being developed jointly in the IETF Policy Framework working group and in the Policy working group of the Distributed Management Task Force.
sections.plainLanguage: The schema is a translation of a separate model document, and the model document is where the meaning of each class is defined. Reading this RFC without it leaves many questions unanswered.

sections.title: The Class Inheritance Hierarchy
sections.content:
All the classes in the schema descend from pcimPolicy, an abstract class that sits under dlm1ManagedElement. Below it, pcimGroup is the abstract class for policy groups, and pcimRule the abstract class for policy rules, each with an auxiliary subclass for attachment to another entry and a structural subclass for a standalone entry.

The rest of the classes in that branch are the three association classes, pcimRuleConditionAssociation, pcimRuleValidityAssociation and pcimRuleActionAssociation, the class pcimPolicyInstance, and the auxiliary class pcimElementAuxClass.

On the other branch, pcimRepository descends through the management system classes from dlm1ManagedSystemElement to dlm1AdminDomain, and has an auxiliary subclass and a structural subclass. The remaining classes are auxiliary: pcimConditionAuxClass, with pcimTPCAuxClass and pcimConditionVendorAuxClass below it; pcimActionAuxClass, with pcimActionVendorAuxClass below it; and on their own, pcimSubtreesPtrAuxClass, pcimGroupContainmentAuxClass and pcimRuleContainmentAuxClass.
sections.plainLanguage: The classes form two trees. One holds policy, groups, rules and the links between them. The other holds conditions, actions, the repository and the extra classes used to point at things.

sections.title: Mapping Classes and Associations
sections.content:
Fifteen of the classes in the schema come directly from the nine corresponding classes in the information model. Names begin with an upper case letter in the information model and a lower case letter in LDAP, because X.500 does not allow class names to begin with an upper case character. The prefix pcim identifies these LDAP classes.

The mapping is one for one for the structural classes: Policy becomes pcimPolicy, PolicyGroup becomes pcimGroup, pcimGroupAuxClass and pcimGroupInstance, and PolicyRule becomes pcimRule, pcimRuleAuxClass and pcimRuleInstance. PolicyCondition becomes pcimConditionAuxClass and PolicyAction becomes pcimActionAuxClass, with the vendor and time period classes below them, and PolicyRepository becomes pcimRepository and its two subclasses.

The associations map to attributes that hold distinguished name references, or to containment in the Directory Information Tree. A group inside a group uses the attribute pcimGroupsAuxContainedSet in pcimGroupContainmentAuxClass, and a rule inside a group uses pcimRulesAuxContainedSet in pcimRuleContainmentAuxClass. A condition in a rule is either containment in the tree, or the attribute pcimRuleConditionList in pcimRule, or pcimConditionDN in pcimRuleConditionAssociation. An action in a rule is handled the same way, with pcimRuleActionList and pcimActionDN. The validity period of a rule uses pcimRuleValidityPeriodList in pcimRule, or, when the period is reusable, pcimTimePeriodConditionDN in pcimRuleValidityAssociation. Conditions, actions and repositories held in the repository itself use tree containment.

Instances in a directory are identified by distinguished names, which give the same kind of hierarchical organisation a file system gives. A distinguished name is a sequence of relative distinguished names, and each relative distinguished name identifies an instance within the context of its immediate superior, the way a filename identifies a file within its folder.

To keep naming flexible, three optional naming attributes are defined. Each structural class has its own naming attribute, so instances of different classes cannot collide even if they are given the same value. The LDAP attribute cn is available through the abstract class pcimPolicy and its subclasses. And a special attribute, orderedCimKeys, holds a value derived from values already present in a CIM policy instance, for implementations that map between native CIM and LDAP representations. Since any of these may be used for naming, implementations must be able to accommodate instances named in any of these ways. The RFC recommends against using two or more of them together to form a multi-part relative distinguished name, because support for that is limited.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of policy object becomes an LDAP class, and each kind of link between objects becomes either a reference to another entry or a position in the directory tree. A policy object can be named by its own attribute, by its common name, or by a key derived from the original model.

sections.title: Rule-Specific and Reusable Conditions
sections.content:
The information model distinguishes between conditions and actions tied to a single policy rule and reusable ones that may be tied to more than one rule. There is no functional difference between them, but there are differences in use and in implementation, and the RFC lists five.

A rule-specific condition or action is naturally removed from the repository when the rule is removed, because it is conceptually attached to the rule. A reusable one is the opposite, because it is referenced rather than owned. Access permissions for a rule-specific condition or action are usually the same as those for the rule, while permissions for a reusable one must be expressible without reference to any rule. Rule-specific conditions and actions need fewer accesses, because they come attached to the rule. They are also meant for a single rule, and as more rules share one, it becomes hard to keep them consistent. A reusable condition or action gives an optimisation, because it only has to be updated once and the rules that point at it are updated automatically.

In an LDAP directory, the difference is realised by where the auxiliary classes sit and by tree containment. A rule-specific condition appears as an entry below the rule in the tree, with the auxiliary class attached to that entry, and the rule holds a distinguished name reference to it. Relying on the tree alone would risk missing conditions that should be there or finding ones that were put there by mistake, so the reference is kept as an option for the designer. The price is that references make it harder to inherit access control information and existence dependency information, and they bring referential integrity questions of their own.

The second way to represent rule-specific conditions and actions is to attach the auxiliary classes straight to the entry representing the rule. A rule treated that way is called simple, and a rule whose conditions or actions live elsewhere is called complex. The distinction is not all or nothing: a rule may attach its conditions to itself and its actions elsewhere, but it must not attach either its conditions or its actions both to itself and to other entries, with one exception, that a rule may reference its validity periods with pcimRuleValidityPeriodList while its other conditions are attached to itself.

Simple rules are efficient but their meaning is limited: all the conditions are combined with AND, and if there is more than one action, no order can be given for them. An administrator who needs conditions combined another way, or actions in a particular order, has to use a complex rule.
sections.plainLanguage: A condition can belong to one rule or be shared by many. Shared ones have to be updated once and every rule sees the change, but they need their own access permissions. A rule that carries its conditions directly is simple and fast, but it can only combine them with AND.

sections.title: Finding and Retrieving Policy Objects
sections.content:
When a Policy Decision Point goes to a directory for the policy objects that apply to the Policy Enforcement Points it serves, it faces two problems. It has to locate and retrieve the directory entries that apply, which may include instances of the schema's classes, subclasses of them, and entries of other classes such as user groups, interfaces and address ranges. And it has to do so efficiently, because retrieval must not become a barrier to scaling. Efficiency has two parts: retrieving only the relevant entries, and retrieving them in as few LDAP calls as possible.

The placement of objects in the tree depends on more than how a decision point will retrieve them, so the schema can only provide a toolkit of classes to help the administrator as the tree is designed. A decision point should be able to take advantage of whatever the administrator built into the tree, but it must be able to fall back on a less efficient method when that is all there is.

The idea behind the optimisation classes is to let a decision point retrieve all the policy objects it needs, and only those objects, in as few calls as possible. That assumes the administrator has enough control over the tree structure to define subtrees for policy information. Without that control the objects can still be retrieved one at a time, but more LDAP operations are needed. The two classes added for this purpose are pcimElementAuxClass and pcimSubtreesPtrAuxClass, which make navigation through the tree and retrieval of the entries there more efficient. The RFC notes that no class in the information model corresponds to them.
sections.plainLanguage: Two extra classes exist purely to make lookups faster. They help a policy server fetch the entries it needs, and only those, in as few requests as possible, when the directory is laid out with policy subtrees.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The schema is not intended to represent any particular system design or implementation, and it is not directly usable in a real world system without the discipline-specific mappings that are works in progress in the Policy Framework working group. Those derivative documents will have to carry more specific security considerations.

The reason the schema is not representative of any real system is that its object classes were designed to be independent of any particular discipline or policy domain. DiffServ and IPsec, for example, are two different policy domains, and the documents that extend the model to each of them derive subclasses from the classes and relationships defined here.

Even so, specific security requirements must be defined for each operational application of the model, because the range of systems and of security requirements is wide. In some deployments the values of certain properties may represent information about scarce and costly resources, and those values must not be disclosed to, or changed by, unauthorised parties. Because this document is the basis for representing policy in an LDAP directory, it points at the directory's own tools for authentication and authorisation.

General LDAP security considerations apply, as documented in RFC 3377, together with the authentication methods in RFC 2829 and the transport layer security extension in RFC 2830. Any security requirement not dealt with in the discipline-specific model documents or in this one must be dealt with in the derivative documents for each discipline.
sections.plainLanguage: The schema is a building block rather than a system, so the security requirements belong to the documents that use it. Where policy values are sensitive, the directory's own authentication and access control should be used to protect them.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA has registered an LDAP object identifier for this specification, 1.3.6.1.1.6, with the name pcimSchema. It is used as a base for identifying the schema elements defined in the document. The IESG is the change controller.

The individual descriptors for the classes and attributes have also been registered, for example pcimPolicy at 1.3.6.1.1.6.1.1, pcimGroup at 1.3.6.1.1.6.1.2, pcimGroupAuxClass at 1.3.6.1.1.6.1.3 and pcimGroupInstance at 1.3.6.1.1.6.1.4. The RFC points to the general IANA considerations for LDAP in RFC 3383.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA has given the schema a base object identifier and registered each class and attribute under it, so that different implementations can refer to the same names.

items.title: Abstract class
items.text: Holds the required properties and cannot itself hold an entry. It is pcimGroup or pcimRule.

items.title: Auxiliary class
items.text: Adds the group or rule to an existing entry rather than creating one of its own.

items.title: Structural class
items.text: Represents the group or rule as an entry of its own in the directory tree.
